entities.name: 2S 300mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A small 2-cell lithium polymer pack, the most common power source for plastic ant vertical spinner and drum builds, giving 7.4V nominal for both a brushless weapon motor and brushed drive motors.

entities.name: 1S 300-500mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A single-cell LiPo pack used in budget or control-focused plastic ants running low-voltage brushed drive motors without a brushless weapon.

entities.name: Printed Hub + TPU Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A 3D-printed rigid hub (PLA+/PETG) with a separately printed TPU tire pressed or glued on, the standard plastic-ant wheel: fully print-and-replace, and legal everywhere since both hub and tire are on the approved plastic list (subject to local TPU rulings).

entities.name: COTS Foam/Silicone Antweight Wheel
entities.summary: An off-the-shelf foam or silicone-tired wheel (e.g. FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) explicitly allowed as a non-plastic-restricted exemption for wheels/tires under most plastic-ant rulesets, offering better and more consistent grip than a printed tire.

entities.name: Small Flanged Ball Bearing (3-4mm bore)
entities.summary: A tiny flanged metal bearing used to support a plastic ant's weapon shaft, explicitly allowed as a metal exemption in every plastic-ant ruleset since bearings are functional hardware, not armor or weapon surface.

entities.name: Small-Diameter Steel Weapon Shaft
entities.summary: A short length of steel drill rod or precision shaft used to carry a plastic weapon disc/drum, exempt from the plastic-only rule as an 'axle' under SPARC-derived language as long as it does not itself act as an armor surface or weapon edge.

entities.name: M2/M3 Screws + Heat-Set Threaded Inserts
entities.summary: Small metal machine screws combined with brass heat-set threaded inserts melted into printed holes, the standard plastic-ant fastening method, explicitly allowed everywhere as long as screw heads on outer surfaces are countersunk or shrouded rather than left proud as de facto armor studs.

entities.name: Micro Slide/Toggle Power Switch
entities.summary: A small mechanical switch used as the required manual main power disconnect, mounted in a printed slot so it can be actuated without contacting moving parts, satisfying the SPARC-derived 15-second manual-disconnect rule.

entities.name: PLA+ (Modified PLA)
entities.summary: A modified PLA filament formulation marketed for improved impact resistance over standard PLA while keeping PLA's easy printability, one of the five materials SPARC and SCAR explicitly name as legal for plastic-ant chassis and weapons.

entities.name: PETG
entities.summary: A tougher, more impact-ductile filament than PLA, widely considered the best default choice for plastic-ant weapon discs/drums and load-bearing chassis members because it bends and absorbs energy rather than shattering.

entities.name: ABS
entities.summary: A strong, impact-resistant, comparatively low-density filament, one of the five universally-legal plastic-ant materials; harder to print reliably (needs an enclosure to prevent warping) but rewards the effort with a lighter, tougher part than PLA.

entities.name: TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)
entities.summary: A rubber-like flexible printable filament popular in the wider combat-robot community for flexible armor panels and wheel tires because it bends and springs back instead of cracking — but it is NOT on the standard SPARC/SCAR approved-material list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's FAQ, making it a key org-to-org variance point in the plastic-ant class.

entities.name: Nylon (Printed)
entities.summary: A tough, wear-resistant, semi-flexible printable nylon filament that, like TPU, sits outside the base SPARC 4.4.1 approved list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's plastic ant FAQ, despite being a popular choice for gears and living-hinge parts in general 3D-printing use.

entities.name: Force Knight — Open-Source 1lb Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A free, open-source 1lb plastic antweight design by community builder Michael K, published as downloadable STL files on Printables and described as intended for SCAR-legal component kits — a good example of the fully-open designs the plastic ant scene shares.

entities.name: CRNZ Antweight Combat Robot Kit
entities.summary: An open-source printable antweight chassis kit published by CombatRoboticsNZ on Thingiverse, designed to be extensible and modular so builders can swap weapon and drive modules without redesigning the whole robot.

entities.name: Legally Distinct — Open-Source 150g UK Drum Spinner Design
entities.summary: A free printable 150g UK-class antweight drum-spinner design by community builder Blessy (published on Thingiverse and documented on Hackaday.io), explicitly built as an homage/iteration on the established UK drum spinner 'Siren' — a clear, verified illustration of how the plastic scene iterates openly on successful designs.

entities.name: Siren (UK 150g Antweight / US Fairyweight)
entities.summary: A 150g UK-Antweight/US-Fairyweight drum-spinner combat robot by designer drcameron, published as free STL files on Thingiverse and Cults3D, well-known enough in the printable-antweight scene to have directly inspired the open-source 'Legally Distinct' drum spinner.

entities.name: Blunt Force Over Cutting
entities.summary: The plastic-ant design principle that, since no metal weapon edge is legal, weapons should be designed to transfer kinetic energy through mass and impact area (denting, cracking, flinging) rather than trying to cut or penetrate as a hardened steel blade would.

entities.name: COTS (Commercial Off-The-Shelf)
entities.summary: Parts bought ready-made rather than fabricated by the builder — motors, ESCs, receivers, bearings, and (per most plastic-ant FAQs) wheels/tires are explicitly allowed as COTS even though they aren't plastic, since the rule targets structural/armor/weapon plastic, not every component.

entities.name: Technical Inspection (Plastic-Only Check)
entities.summary: The pre-event safety/legality check where an event official visually inspects a plastic ant for compliance: verifying the chassis/armor/weapon are printed plastic, checking that any metal fasteners are countersunk/shrouded rather than proud, and looking for banned materials like TPU, nylon, or composite reinforcement layered into a printed part.

entities.name: Sacrificial Armor Panel
entities.summary: A deliberately weaker, easily-detachable printed panel placed over a robot's vulnerable areas so that a hit cracks/pops off the panel (a 5-minute reprint) instead of transmitting damage into the main chassis or electronics bay.

entities.name: Modular Bolt-On Section
entities.summary: A design pattern where the chassis is split into independently printed, bolt-together sections (e.g. separate front wedge, weapon pod, and drive base) so a single damaged section can be reprinted and swapped without remaking the whole robot.

entities.name: Printed-In Flexure
entities.summary: A thin, deliberately flexible section printed as part of a single larger piece (rather than a separate hinge with a pin) that acts as a spring or hinge — used in plastic ants for snap-fit panels, simple lifter linkages, and shock-absorbing mounts without adding a metal hinge part.

entities.name: Wall Count / Perimeters
entities.summary: The number of solid outer print loops (walls) surrounding a part's infill; combat-ready plastic ant parts typically use significantly more walls (5-8+) than a decorative print (2-3) because the solid perimeter, not the infill, carries most of an impact load.

entities.name: Infill Percentage (Combat Printing)
entities.summary: The proportion of a printed part's interior that is filled with a lattice pattern rather than left hollow; competitive plastic ant chassis parts commonly run 40-100% infill with a gyroid or cubic pattern, well above the 15-20% typical of non-structural prints, trading weight for toughness within the 454g budget.

entities.name: Layer Adhesion Anisotropy
entities.summary: The property that FDM-printed plastic is much stronger for forces applied parallel to its print layers than for forces trying to pull layers apart (perpendicular to them); the single most important physical fact plastic ant designers work around, driving choices about print orientation for weapons, wedges and shafts.

entities.name: Annealing (3D Print Post-Processing)
entities.summary: A post-print heat-treatment process (baking a printed part at a temperature below its melt point, sometimes packed in sand or salt to limit warping) that can meaningfully increase a part's layer strength and heat resistance; explicitly permitted post-processing under SCAR's plastic ant FAQ.

entities.name: Five-Minute Pit Repair
entities.summary: The plastic-ant repair philosophy of designing bolt-on, single-piece printed sub-assemblies so that a cracked wedge, wheel, or weapon can be swapped for a spare printed at home in under five minutes between matches, rather than requiring on-site fabrication or welding as a metal repair might.

entities.name: Robot Ruckus
entities.summary: A US SPARC-compliant combat robotics event run in conjunction with Maker Faire Orlando, popular with antweight and plastic-antweight builders. Insect weight classes (fairyweight/antweight/beetleweight) run double-elimination, while the larger 12lb/30lb/30lb-super-class divisions use a pools/Swiss fight format instead.

entities.name: SoCal Attack Robots (SCAR)
entities.summary: A Southern California combat robot organization/event series with one of the most detailed published Plastic Ant rulesets and FAQs in the US scene, explicitly naming approved filament brands and banning TPU/nylon.

entities.name: Bot Blast
entities.summary: An annual US insectweight-focused combat robotics event running a modified SPARC ruleset. Its main deviations from stock SPARC are a modified double-elimination format, a ban on autonomous robots, an immediate KO (at official discretion) for any robot with an exposed/damaged LiPo battery, and simplified judging criteria versus full SPARC judging.

entities.name: National Havoc Robot League (NHRL)
entities.summary: A major US combat robot league best known for its livestreamed 3lb (beetleweight) and 12/30lb events; NHRL itself is not the primary home of the 1lb plastic ant class (its own plastic-material class is Plastic Beetleweight), but many smaller 'NHRL-adjacent' local and remote-competition circuits run 1lb plastic ant undercards using a similar remote-competition/streamed format.

entities.name: FingerTech Robotics
entities.summary: A Canadian combat-robot parts supplier whose wheels, motors, and hubs are explicitly named as legal COTS options in plastic ant FAQs, making it one of the standard go-to sources for the non-plastic-exempt parts of a plastic ant build.

entities.name: Spinning Weapon Tip Speed
entities.summary: The standard combat-robotics formula for converting a spinning weapon's no-load RPM and diameter into tip speed in feet per second, taken verbatim from SPARC's Robot Construction Specifications (used to set/verify Sportsman-class and open-air tip-speed limits) and used informally by builders in every weight class, plastic ant included, to sanity-check a weapon design before it's built.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Wedge
entities.summary: The wedge wins the initial engagement but has no way to convert it into a win, while the spinner only needs one clean hit.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: The horizontal's reach and sweep attack the vertical's exposed weapon and wheels before the vertical can close to its own engagement range.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The undercutter strikes below the vertical spinner's weapon arc, hitting wheels and ground clearance where the vertical cannot defend.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Drum spinner
entities.summary: Both hit upward, but the drum's larger diameter and lower mounting give it better bite, so it usually lands first in a head-on exchange.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Control bot
entities.summary: The control bot has no answer to accumulating damage, and at 1 lb a few clean upward hits end the match.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Grabber
entities.summary: If the grabber closes on the spinner the match is effectively over, but surviving the approach against a live weapon is genuinely hard.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Flipper
entities.summary: The flipper attacks from underneath, which is the one direction a vertical spinner cannot defend, and a flip against a non-invertible spinner ends it.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Hammer
entities.summary: The spinner accumulates energy over seconds; the hammer only has its swing arc. The energy difference is decisive at 1 lb.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Thwackbot
entities.summary: The thwackbot cannot attack and manoeuvre at once; the spinner simply engages while it is spinning up.

entities.name: Vertical spinner vs Rammer
entities.summary: A 454 g ram carries very little energy, and the rammer must close to contact range where the weapon lives.

entities.name: Wedge vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: The bar sweeps harmlessly over a wedge that touches the floor, while the wedge lifts the spinner and removes its traction.

entities.name: Wedge vs Shell spinner
entities.summary: A shell spinner's weapon is its outer edge, which a good wedge slides beneath; once lifted, a shell has no recovery.

entities.name: Wedge vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The undercutter's whole purpose is beating wedges — it strikes below the wedge's leading edge, where the wedge offers no protection.

entities.name: Wedge vs Drum spinner
entities.summary: The drum's low mounting and large diameter let it engage a wedge's edge rather than riding over it.

entities.name: Wedge vs Control bot
entities.summary: Two control robots meeting is decided almost entirely by ground clearance, edge quality and driving.

entities.name: Wedge vs Hammer
entities.summary: A hammer has to be nearly touching to strike; a wedge that gets under removes its footing before the arm comes down.

entities.name: Horizontal bar spinner vs Shell spinner
entities.summary: Two horizontal weapons meeting is largely a coin-flip decided by which has more energy and better tooth geometry; the bar usually has higher tip speed.

entities.name: Horizontal bar spinner vs Drum spinner
entities.summary: The horizontal's reach lets it strike the drum's supports and wheels before the drum closes to its own range.

entities.name: Horizontal bar spinner vs Forkbot
entities.summary: Hinged forks float on the floor and slide under the bar's sweep, which passes over them harmlessly.

entities.name: Drum spinner vs Control bot
entities.summary: A drum's bite means it engages a control bot reliably, and repeated upward hits break wheels and armour.

entities.name: Drum spinner vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The drum's low front can engage the undercutter's bar and supports, and its bite works even against a low target.

entities.name: Flipper vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: The flipper needs to close and get under, and the bar's reach punishes the approach.

entities.name: Flipper vs Control bot
entities.summary: A control bot with no weapon has nothing to deter the flipper's approach, and a flip removes its only asset — ground contact.

entities.name: Flipper vs Invertible brick
entities.summary: Flipping an invertible robot achieves nothing — it drives away the same either way up.

entities.name: Grabber vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: Once clamped, a horizontal spinner's weapon cannot reach the grabber at all, and its energy becomes useless.

entities.name: Grabber vs Wedge
entities.summary: A wedge gets under the grabber before the jaws can close, and a lifted grabber cannot grip anything.

entities.name: Hammer vs Control bot
entities.summary: Against an opponent with no weapon, the hammer can close safely and work on the top armour at leisure.

entities.name: Thwackbot vs Control bot
entities.summary: The thwackbot's tail outranges a weaponless pushing robot and can damage wheels.

entities.name: Multibot vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: Each half of a multibot is small and fragile, and a spinner only needs to destroy one at a time.

entities.name: Multibot vs Wedge
entities.summary: A single wedge can only face one direction; two robots attacking from opposite sides defeat that.

entities.name: Armour bot vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: A spinner's energy has to go somewhere, and against heavy compliant armour a large share goes back into the spinner.

entities.name: Wedge + spinner hybrid vs Wedge
entities.summary: The hybrid matches the wedge's ground game with its own wedgelets, then adds damage the wedge cannot answer.

entities.name: Wedge + spinner hybrid vs Undercutter
entities.summary: The hybrid's advantage is its wedgelets, and the undercutter attacks below exactly that line.

entities.name: Melty brain vs Wedge
entities.summary: The melty presents a spinning face from every direction, so the wedge has no safe approach angle.

entities.name: Beater bar vs Control bot
entities.summary: Even a modest beater bar accumulates damage that a weaponless robot cannot answer.

entities.name: Beater bar vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: Same damage vector, far more energy on the vertical spinner's side.

entities.name: Shell spinner vs Control bot
entities.summary: There is no safe angle to push a shell spinner from, and its energy is enormous.

entities.name: Lifter vs Vertical spinner
entities.summary: The lifter must get under to work, and the approach exposes its arm to the weapon.

entities.name: Lifter vs Horizontal bar spinner
entities.summary: A lifter with a wedge-quality edge gets under the sweep, then carries the spinner where it likes.

entities.name: Rammer vs Control bot
entities.summary: Two weaponless robots — the one with better traction, edge and driving wins.

entities.name: Judging Criteria
entities.summary: When a match goes the distance, judges score it — usually on damage, aggression and control.

entities.name: Driving Practice
entities.summary: Deliberate practice at driving, which decides more antweight matches than design does.

entities.name: Scouting
entities.summary: Watching your bracket before you fight it, and adapting your configuration.

entities.name: Configuration Swap
entities.summary: Changing the robot between matches to counter a specific opponent.

entities.name: Weigh-In
entities.summary: The check that your robot is inside the class weight limit.

entities.name: Mass-toward-the-rim effect on MOI
entities.summary: For a fixed total mass and fixed outer radius, moving material from the center toward the rim increases moment of inertia and stored energy without adding weight -- the single biggest lever in weapon geometry.

entities.name: Tooth count does not change stored energy
entities.summary: Splitting a fixed tooth mass at a fixed radius into more teeth does not change the weapon's moment of inertia or stored kinetic energy -- tooth count only changes bite depth and hit frequency, which is a commonly confused point.

entities.name: Drum wall thickness vs MOI (thin-wall vs thick-wall drum)
entities.summary: For a fixed drum outer diameter and total mass, a thinner wall (mass pushed toward the outside) gives meaningfully more MOI than a thick-walled drum of the same weight -- the drum-spinner version of the mass-toward-rim principle.

entities.name: Tip speed vs diameter at a fixed motor RPM
entities.summary: At a fixed weapon RPM, a larger-diameter disc gives higher tip speed and more stored energy, but its MOI grows with the square of radius, which slows spin-up and demands more motor torque -- the core diameter-vs-thickness tradeoff for vertical discs.

entities.name: Effective bite path length vs tooth rake angle
entities.summary: A swept-back (raked) tooth follows a longer path through the opponent's material for the same straight-line bite depth, trading peak impact force for a longer, lower-force engagement -- a simplified geometric model for comparing tooth profiles.

entities.name: Effective bite against an angled wedge surface
entities.summary: Striking a sloped wedge face instead of a flat vertical face reduces the normal (penetrating) component of a spinner's bite, which is why steep, aggressive wedges are an effective spinner counter and low, shallow wedges preserve more of the attacker's bite.

entities.name: Residual unbalance and shaking force vs RPM
entities.summary: A small leftover unbalance (mass times its offset from the rotation axis) produces a centrifugal shaking force that grows with the square of RPM, which is why fast antweight spinners need much tighter balance tolerances than slow ones.

entities.name: Hub fastener shear capacity vs weapon torque
entities.summary: The torque a bolted or set-screw hub can transmit is set by the shear strength of its fasteners times their number and bolt-circle radius; comparing this to the weapon motor's stall torque shows whether the hub -- or something else -- is the weak link.

entities.name: Cantilevered shaft bending stress under impact load
entities.summary: A weapon shaft supported by only one bearing (cantilevered) sees bending stress proportional to the impact force times the unsupported length; shortening that length or adding a second support point cuts stress dramatically and is the main structural argument for double-bearing shaft support.

entities.name: Tooth profile
entities.summary: The shape of a spinning weapon's cutting/striking edge in cross-section -- common profiles for antweights include a simple radial chisel tooth, a hooked or claw profile that grabs and lifts, and a blunt flat-faced tooth used mainly for pure kinetic hammering rather than cutting.

entities.name: Rake angle
entities.summary: The angle of a tooth's leading face relative to a purely radial line from the center of rotation. Zero rake (radial) gives the most direct, highest peak-force impact; a swept-back (negative) rake trades some peak force and bite depth for a longer, gentler engagement and less shock loading on the tooth root and bearings; a forward (positive/aggressive) rake can dig in harder but is far more prone to chipping or snapping on a hard hit.

entities.name: Hardened tooth insert
entities.summary: A separate hardened-steel (or carbide) tooth bolted, pinned, press-fit, or welded into a softer weapon body, rather than machining the whole weapon from one hard billet. Lets the body be made from tougher, easier-to-machine, or lighter material (aluminum, mild steel, even plastic on plastic-antweights) while only the actual striking edge needs to be hard and wear-resistant.

entities.name: Monolithic weapon construction
entities.summary: A weapon machined or cut from a single piece of material with no separate tooth inserts -- the whole disc, bar, or drum is the same hardness throughout. Simpler and lighter (no fasteners or pockets), but a chip or crack in the edge is a chip or crack in the entire weapon, and the whole piece must be through-hardened or case-hardened as one part.

entities.name: Canted bar spinner
entities.summary: A bar spinner whose blade(s) are angled slightly out of the pure vertical or horizontal plane, so impacts impart some off-axis (up/down or sideways) force in addition to the main rotational hit. Used to try to pop an opponent up off the ground, deflect strikes away from the canted bot's own frame, or reduce head-on lockups between two similar spinners; the tradeoff is a less efficient direct hit and a slightly harder weapon to balance because its mass is no longer confined to a single plane.

entities.name: Egg-shaped (eccentric) drum
entities.summary: A drum spinner whose cross-section is not a true circle but an oval or egg shape, so the effective radius to the cutting edge -- and therefore the bite depth and impact timing -- varies through the rotation. Intended to deliver a mix of a 'sweeping' lower-force pass and a harder-hitting peak strike each revolution, at the cost of being much harder to balance than a true cylindrical drum and requiring a correspondingly variable ground-clearance envelope.

entities.name: Support ring / bearing arrangement for shell spinners
entities.summary: The stationary structure (often a large-diameter thin bearing, a bearing race machined into the frame, or several small support bearings/rollers riding on the inside of the ring) that keeps a shell spinner's thin outer ring running true and prevents it from deflecting or walking off-axis at high rpm. Because a shell spinner's entire weapon mass sits far from the center as a thin ring (see the mass-toward-rim formula), the ring itself is relatively flexible and depends on this support structure -- not just the drive bearing -- to stay round and balanced under load.

entities.name: Weapon ground clearance
entities.summary: The gap between the lowest point of a spinning weapon (or its housing) and the arena floor. Ground clearance controls how much of an opponent's low wedge or skirt the weapon can actually reach: too much clearance and low wedges simply slide underneath the weapon untouched; too little and the weapon risks striking the floor itself, which can shatter teeth, stall the motor, or violate event floor-damage rules. Undercutters push this to the minimum practical gap; overhead horizontal spinners are largely unaffected by it since they strike above the frame.

entities.name: Floor interaction (undercutters)
entities.summary: The defining trait of undercutter weapons: the spinning weapon sits low, near or partly below the drive wheels, so it can get underneath an opponent's wedge or skirt where an overhead weapon cannot reach. This close floor proximity means undercutters take more incidental damage from arena floor imperfections and screws, generate sparks/debris that can be a spectator and rules concern, and generally need a slightly more durable, lower running weapon speed than an equivalent overhead design to survive routine floor contact.

entities.name: Keyway
entities.summary: A machined slot cut lengthwise into both a shaft and its mating hub, into which a separate key (a small steel bar) is fitted so the two parts rotate together positively instead of relying on friction. Transmits high torque and survives shock loads far better than a set screw, but the slot itself is a stress concentration that can become the shaft's weak point, and cutting a clean small keyway in an ant-scale shaft (often 4-8 mm diameter) requires more precise machining than a set-screw flat or a broached hex.

entities.name: Broached hex bore
entities.summary: A hub or pulley bored with an internal hexagonal hole that slides onto a matching hexagonal section of shaft, giving a positive, low-part-count torque connection without a separate key. Very common on antweight weapon pulleys and sprockets because a short length of hex stock (or a shaft with a hex section machined/ground onto it) is cheap and simple, and the hex engagement handles shock loads much better than a round-bore set-screw hub, though it still needs some axial retention (a screw, retaining ring, or shoulder) to keep the hub from sliding off the shaft.

entities.name: Set-screw hub
entities.summary: The simplest and lightest weapon-to-shaft attachment: a round bore with one or more screws (often against a flat ground into the shaft) that clamp the hub on by friction and slight shaft deformation. Cheap, adjustable, and easy to remove, but it is a friction joint -- under the shock torque of a hard weapon impact it can slip on the shaft, throwing the weapon's timing/balance off or losing drive entirely, which is why harder-hitting antweight builds often upgrade to a keyway or broached hex once set-screw slip becomes a recurring failure.

entities.name: Static balance
entities.summary: Balancing a rotating part so its center of mass lies exactly on the rotation axis, checked by letting the part rest freely on a level, low-friction axis (a balancing mandrel) and seeing whether it stays put in any orientation or always rotates to put a heavy spot at the bottom. Sufficient for thin, disc-like weapons where essentially all the mass sits in one plane perpendicular to the shaft; the standard, low-cost balancing method for most antweight vertical-disc and shell-spinner builds.

entities.name: Dynamic balance
entities.summary: Balancing a rotating part in two separate planes along its length, not just its overall center of mass -- necessary for weapons with significant length along the rotation axis (long bars, wide drums) where the part can be statically balanced (center of mass on-axis) yet still wobble in operation because the mass distribution at one end differs from the other, creating a rocking couple. Checking this at the hobbyist level typically means balancing each end/plane of the weapon separately (e.g., weighing/trimming each half of a bar independently) rather than true multi-plane balancing-machine measurement.

entities.name: Balancing mandrel / balancing stand
entities.summary: A simple hobbyist static-balancing setup: the weapon is mounted on a precision shaft (mandrel) or its own shaft, which is then rested on a pair of level, low-friction supports -- hardened knife edges, a set of unloaded bearings, or even two parallel round rods. Gravity rotates the assembly until the heavy side settles at the bottom; that spot is marked, and material is removed there (or added to the opposite side) and the check repeated until the weapon stays put in any rotational position, indicating the center of mass is on the shaft axis.

entities.name: Bell separation (failure mode)
entities.summary: A failure mode specific to dead-shaft weapon mounts where the drive pulley/sprocket ('bell') is bonded, pinned, or pressed onto the spinning weapon body: a hard impact shock-loads that bond/pin joint and the bell separates from the weapon, either slipping in place (losing drive) or fully detaching. Usually fixed by adding mechanical retention beyond adhesive alone -- screws, a broached hex or keyed interface, or a press fit backed by a positive stop -- rather than relying on bonding strength alone to survive combat shock loads.

entities.name: Hub slip (failure mode)
entities.summary: A failure mode where a weapon's hub rotates relative to its shaft under impact shock, most commonly on set-screw hubs biting onto a smooth round shaft. The immediate symptom is the weapon's teeth ending up in the wrong angular position relative to where the driver expects them, or complete loss of drive to the weapon; repeated slip also gradually damages (galls/rounds) the shaft surface the set screw bites into, making the problem worse over time. The standard fix is a positive-drive interface (keyway or hex broach) rather than tightening the set screw harder.

entities.name: Bent shaft (failure mode)
entities.summary: Permanent plastic deformation of a weapon shaft from bending loads that exceeded the shaft material's yield strength, usually from a hard impact combined with a long unsupported (cantilevered) length or an undersized/soft shaft material. Symptoms are a weapon that now runs visibly off-true, vibrates even after rebalancing, and puts abnormal radial load into its bearings; the fix is a shorter unsupported span (a second bearing closer to the weapon), a larger-diameter shaft, or a harder alloy shaft material, not just re-straightening the existing shaft, which rarely restores full strength.

entities.name: Exploded bearing (failure mode)
entities.summary: Catastrophic bearing failure in a weapon assembly, where the ball cage shatters, balls escape, or a shield/seal blows out from a single hard radial impact or from sustained vibration due to an unbalanced weapon. Small ant-scale bearings (623/626/688 class) have limited shock load capacity, so this failure is common after either a single very hard direct hit that was transmitted straight through a weapon shaft into its bearing, or slow fatigue from running an out-of-balance weapon for many matches; flanged bearings and a snug, properly-sized bore/shaft fit reduce (but do not eliminate) the risk.

entities.name: Moment arm (hammers/axes)
entities.summary: For a hammer or axe weapon, the distance from the pivot to the head's center of mass (and to its impact point). A longer moment arm gives the head a higher tip speed and more kinetic energy for the same swing torque and angular acceleration, but also increases the weapon's MOI (which scales with the square of that distance), demanding more torque/time to swing and putting more bending stress on the pivot and its bearings/shaft during the strike.

entities.name: Edge preparation (static weapons)
entities.summary: The sharpening angle, edge geometry, and heat treatment applied to a fork, spike, or wedge's leading edge. A thin, low included angle bites into opponent material more easily but chips or rolls over on a hard impact; a thicker, more obtuse angle survives repeated hard hits better but requires more closing force/speed to penetrate at all. Hardening the edge (case hardening a mild-steel wedge lip, or using a pre-hardened tool steel insert) lets a bot keep a thinner, more aggressive angle without it deforming on contact.

entities.name: 623 bearing (3x10x4mm)
entities.summary: A very small deep-groove ball bearing, 3mm bore x 10mm OD x 4mm width, used on the smallest antweight and plastic-antweight weapon and drive shafts where every gram counts.

entities.name: 626 bearing (6x19x6mm)
entities.summary: A common small deep-groove ball bearing, 6mm bore x 19mm OD x 6mm width, a popular middle-ground choice for antweight weapon shafts needing more shaft diameter (bending strength) than a 623 without jumping to a heavier bearing.

entities.name: 688 bearing (8x16x5mm)
entities.summary: A common small deep-groove ball bearing, 8mm bore x 16mm OD x 5mm width. A popular choice for antweight weapon shafts and dead-shaft drum/disc mounts because the 8mm bore supports a noticeably stiffer, stronger shaft than a 623/626 in a still-compact OD.

entities.name: Flanged bearing (F-series, e.g. F688/F626)
entities.summary: A standard bearing with an added outer flange (e.g. F688, F626) that seats against the face of a bore instead of needing a shoulder or retaining ring, commonly used in dead-shaft weapon 'bells' so the bearing self-locates and resists walking axially under impact side-loads.

entities.name: Bronze bushing (plain bearing)
entities.summary: A solid or sintered bronze sleeve used as a plain (non-ball) bearing on a weapon or drive shaft. Cheaper and more tolerant of debris and minor misalignment than a ball bearing, at the cost of higher friction and a lower practical RPM ceiling.

entities.name: Set-screw hub
entities.summary: A round-bore aluminum or steel hub clamped to a shaft with one or more radial set screws, typically biting onto a flat ground into the shaft. The lightest and simplest weapon attachment method for antweights, but a friction joint that can slip under hard shock loads (see term-hub-slip).

entities.name: Clamping (split/pinch) hub
entities.summary: A hub with a slit and a clamping screw that squeezes the full bore diameter down onto the shaft, rather than a set screw biting a single point. Grips more of the shaft's circumference, avoids denting/deforming the shaft the way a point-contact set screw can, and holds up somewhat better under shock -- still a friction joint, so still weaker than a keyway or hex broach under hard impacts.

entities.name: 7075-T6 aluminum (hubs / light disc bodies)
entities.summary: A high-strength aerospace-grade aluminum alloy used in antweight builds for hubs, backing plates, and lighter-duty disc bodies where weight savings matter more than maximum impact toughness -- generally paired with a hardened steel tooth insert rather than used bare as a striking edge.

entities.name: UHMW polyethylene (plastic-antweight weapon body)
entities.summary: Ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene sheet or rod, a tough, low-friction, impact-resistant plastic that is a legal weapon and structural material for plastic-antweight classes where metal weapon bodies are restricted; used for discs, drum bodies, and wedge scoops.

entities.name: Titanium 6Al-4V (lightweight high-strength tips/bars)
entities.summary: A titanium alloy offering roughly steel-level strength at about 60% of the density, used in weight-critical antweight spinner tips, bars, or hubs where every gram saved can be redirected into more weapon mass at the rim or more battery/drivetrain budget.

entities.name: 1104 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: Tiny 11mm-diameter, 4mm-tall stator motor from the FPV whoop/toothpick world, used as an ultra-light vertical spinner or micro-drum motor on plastic antweights and fairyweights.

entities.name: 1106 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 11mm x 6mm stator motor, one step up from 1104 in stator height/torque, used for slightly heavier plastic-ant vertical spinners and paddle weapons.

entities.name: 1204 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 12mm-diameter, 4mm-tall stator motor, a common toothpick-drone motor repurposed as a plastic-ant or fairyweight vertical spinner/beater motor.

entities.name: 1306 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 13mm x 6mm stator motor originally built for FPV micro racing quads (2-3 inch props); a very common plastic-ant and light 1 lb weapon motor because of its wide KV range and cheap availability.

entities.name: 1404 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 14mm x 4mm stator motor, a step above 1306 in diameter (more torque, similar height); used on heavier plastic ants and light 1 lb spinners.

entities.name: 1408 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 14mm x 8mm stator motor, one of the most popular 'toothpick' drone sizes; a very common choice for 1 lb antweight vertical spinners, small drums, and light bars where a 1806 is too heavy.

entities.name: 1806 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 18mm x 6mm stator motor from the older 200-250 class mini-quad era; a long-running staple antweight weapon motor thanks to its 3mm shaft and 16x16mm M3 mount that make it easy to bolt straight to a hub or pulley.

entities.name: 2004 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 20mm x 4mm cinewhoop-derived stator, a lighter-weight alternative in the 20xx bracket for antweight builders who want a bit more diameter/torque than 1806 without the weight of a 2205+.

entities.name: 2205 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 5mm stator, one of the definitive FPV racing-motor sizes and a very common 1 lb antweight vertical-disc/bar weapon motor because of its balance of torque, RPM range, and cheap availability.

entities.name: 2206 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 6mm stator, a taller/torquier sibling of the 2205, popular in freestyle-quad builds and equally popular as an antweight bar or disc spinner motor.

entities.name: 2207 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 22mm x 7mm stator, one of the most common freestyle/racing FPV motor sizes and a direct antweight favorite; Repeat Robotics' antweight hubmotor is built on this stator size for plug-and-play direct-drive weapons.

entities.name: 2306 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 23mm x 6mm stator, the long-time standard 5-inch mini-quad motor size; used in antweights as a slightly larger-diameter alternative to the 22xx family for bar and drum spinners needing more torque.

entities.name: 2504 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 25mm x 4mm stator; a lighter member of the 25xx family used where extra diameter (torque) is wanted without jumping fully into 28xx weight, common on heavier 1 lb bar/drum builds pushing into light-beetle territory.

entities.name: 2508 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 25mm x 8mm stator, a tall/high-torque long-range and heavy-lift drone motor; in combat it is a low-KV, high-torque option for belt-reduced 1 lb drums and bars that need bite more than raw tip speed.

entities.name: 2806 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 6mm stator, entry point of the 28xx family; used on heavy 1 lb builds and as a light-beetleweight crossover weapon motor, usually belt-driven to keep tip speed in range at low KV.

entities.name: 2812 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 12mm stator, a very tall/torquey size from the heavy-lift/cinelifter drone world; occasionally used on the heaviest 1 lb builds or light beetles as a high-torque belt-driven weapon motor.

entities.name: 2814 brushless motor (weapon)
entities.summary: 28mm x 14mm stator, the classic heavy-lift/heavy-ant-beetle-crossover size; the Cobra 2814 in particular is a well-known belt-drive weapon motor used across heavy 1 lb and light beetleweight spinners.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics 2822 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: Purpose-built antweight weapon outrunner on a 28mm-diameter, 22mm-length can, sold specifically for direct-drive antweight spinners rather than repurposed from a drone; widely regarded as one of the most durable off-the-shelf antweight weapon motors.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics 2207 Battle Ready Hubmotor
entities.summary: A 2207-stator combat hubmotor sold as a complete direct-drive weapon solution for antweights: the weapon hub/disc bolts straight to the motor bell, eliminating a separate shaft-and-bearing weapon assembly.

entities.name: Repeat Robotics Scalar Antweight Weapon Motor (2305)
entities.summary: A 23mm-stator-class purpose-built antweight weapon motor with an oversized ~28.2mm outer bell for extra rotor mass/flywheel effect relative to its stator size.

entities.name: RDY-5022 Antweight Hubmotor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics antweight direct-drive hubmotor, offered in 1100kv and 1700kv windings, sized for antweight vertical spinners at typical 3-4S antweight voltages.

entities.name: RDY-5536 Beetleweight Hubmotor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics beetleweight-class direct-drive hubmotor, offered in 900kv and 1200kv windings; relevant to antweights mainly as the upper end of the size ladder / heavy-ant crossover reference point.

entities.name: JCR-4935 Horizontal Spinner Motor
entities.summary: Just 'Cuz Robotics 1000kv motor specifically marketed for horizontal spinners (bars/blades spun about a vertical-ish or horizontal axis with high aerodynamic drag), where a lower KV is used to keep current sane against drag.

entities.name: BadAss 23-series 2315 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: A 23mm-diameter, 15mm-length belt-drive weapon motor at 1480kv, cited as a common antweight/heavy-ant belt-drive option that trades some direct-drive simplicity for a taller, torquier stator than typical 23xx drone motors.

entities.name: Turbo 2830 Weapon Motor
entities.summary: A 28mm-diameter, 30mm-length belt-drive weapon motor at 1300kv; one of the largest commonly cited motors used at the antweight/beetleweight belt-drive crossover for high-torque drums and bars.

entities.name: Required motor KV from target tip speed and battery voltage
entities.summary: Back-solves the motor KV (or KV x gear-ratio) needed to hit a target tip speed on a given battery voltage, the single most common weapon-motor sizing question in the hobby.

entities.name: Rotational kinetic energy stored in a spinning weapon
entities.summary: Computes the joules of kinetic energy stored in a weapon flywheel from its moment of inertia and angular velocity -- the number that actually predicts damage potential, not RPM alone.

entities.name: Weapon spin-up time estimate from torque and MOI
entities.summary: Estimates the time to bring a weapon from rest to full speed given the weapon's moment of inertia and the motor's average available accelerating torque over that speed range -- the calculation that explains why an underpowered motor loses matches before the fight even starts.

entities.name: Weapon motor peak and steady electrical power draw
entities.summary: Estimates electrical power draw during weapon spin-up (near stall) versus steady-state windmilling, used to size battery C-rating and ESC current headroom.

entities.name: RPM to angular velocity (rad/s) conversion
entities.summary: Simple unit conversion used throughout weapon-motor sizing math to move between RPM (what motor/ESC specs use) and rad/s (what physics formulas for torque, power and kinetic energy need).

entities.name: KV (motor velocity constant)
entities.summary: The unloaded RPM a brushless motor spins per volt applied, in RPM/V. Determines top speed for a given voltage, but says nothing about torque or power by itself -- a motor's stator size and winding resistance matter just as much.

entities.name: Stator volume (diameter x height)
entities.summary: The product of a brushless motor's stator diameter and stator height/stack length, encoded directly in FPV motor names (e.g. '2207' = 22mm diameter x 7mm height). Stator volume is the single best predictor of how much torque and continuous power a motor can produce, because it sets how much copper and iron can be packed in to carry current and hold magnetic flux without saturating.

entities.name: Back-EMF (counter-electromotive force)
entities.summary: The voltage a spinning motor generates that opposes the applied drive voltage, proportional to RPM and inversely proportional to KV (Back-EMF volts = RPM / KV). As a weapon motor spins up, rising back-EMF is what makes available current -- and therefore torque -- fall off as speed increases, producing the classic linear torque-speed line.

entities.name: Outrunner vs inrunner
entities.summary: Outrunner motors spin the outer magnet-lined bell/can around a fixed inner stator (the common FPV/drone layout); inrunner motors spin a small magnet rotor inside a fixed outer stator can. Outrunners dominate weapon-motor use because their larger effective rotor radius gives more torque per amp and the bell itself doubles as a flywheel/weapon-mounting surface.

entities.name: Demagnetization (weapon motor failure)
entities.summary: Permanent partial loss of magnetic strength in a motor's rotor magnets, caused by driving current far beyond the motor's rated stall current (common during a hard weapon-vs-weapon or weapon-vs-wall impact stall) or by sustained overheating past the magnet's Curie-adjacent temperature limit. A demagnetized motor permanently loses torque and top KV-equivalent speed even after the fault current stops.

entities.name: Fairyweight (150g)
entities.summary: The smallest weight class in common use, capped at 150 grams (about 0.33 lb). In the US/SPARC world it is called Fairyweight; confusingly, this exact 150g limit is what British builders call 'Antweight', which is far lighter than the US 1lb antweight. It is a popular entry point because parts are cheap and damage is minimal.

entities.name: Antweight (1 lb)
entities.summary: The classic North American entry class, capped at 1 lb (454 g). It is the most-run class at US and Canadian events (SPARC, RoboGames, Motorama, Robot Ruckus, Bot Blast) and is roughly three times heavier than the UK 'Antweight' (150 g), a naming collision that trips up new builders reading rules from the wrong region.

entities.name: Beetleweight (3 lb)
entities.summary: A 3 lb (1.36 kg) class, the second most popular class in the US after antweight, and one of NHRL's three official divisions. It allows meaningfully more powerful weapons and drivetrains than antweight while still being affordable and easy to transport.

entities.name: Plastic Beetleweight
entities.summary: The 3 lb equivalent of plastic antweight: robots must be built almost entirely from approved 3D-printable plastics rather than metal. Less common than plastic antweight but growing at the same regional US events that run plastic-only brackets.

entities.name: Hobbyweight (12 lb)
entities.summary: A 12 lb (5.44 kg) middle-tier class, one of NHRL's three flagship divisions and a common SPARC class. It's a step up in cost and danger from beetleweight, generally viewed as an intermediate builder's class.

entities.name: Featherweight (30 lb)
entities.summary: A 30 lb (13.6 kg) class, NHRL's largest flagship division and a long-standing SPARC/RoboGames class. Featherweight fights are visibly more destructive than smaller classes and require more serious safety gear and containment.

entities.name: Lightweight (60 lb)
entities.summary: A 60 lb (27.2 kg) class run mainly by SPARC and RoboGames. It sits between the popular small hobby classes and the TV-scale heavyweights, requiring real machine-shop fabrication and industrial-grade components.

entities.name: Middleweight (120 lb)
entities.summary: A 120 lb (54.4 kg) class run by SPARC and RoboGames, sitting just below the TV-scale heavyweight class. Robots at this size need hydraulic/pneumatic or large brushless weapon systems and significant safety infrastructure.

entities.name: Heavyweight (220-250 lb)
entities.summary: The top-tier 'TV weight' class. BattleBots' modern single division caps at 250 lb (113 kg) ready-to-fight, while SPARC's traditional heavyweight class is 220 lb (100 kg); RoboGames also runs a 250 lb class plus a heavier walking-bonus tier. These robots require professional-grade fabrication, hydraulics/large brushless weapons, and are only run at events with heavy-duty arenas.

entities.name: SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat)
entities.summary: SPARC is the dominant unified US/international rule set for hobby-scale combat robotics. A single 'SPARC-legal' build is accepted at essentially every SPARC-compliant event worldwide, covering weight classes from fairyweight (150g) up to heavyweight (220 lb), plastic-class material rules, weight bonuses for walkers/shufflers, multibot/clusterbot rules, and standardized safety requirements.

entities.name: NHRL Open Rules (National Havoc Robot League)
entities.summary: NHRL runs the largest recurring US combat robotics series (Franklin, MA) across exactly three weight classes: 3lb (beetleweight), 12lb (hobbyweight), and 30lb (featherweight). It uses a qualifying-then-bracket tournament format, mandatory weapon locks and radio failsafe testing, and pays cash prizes, which distinguishes it from most hobbyist-only events.

entities.name: RoboGames Combat Robot Rules
entities.summary: RoboGames (formerly ROBOlympics) is a large annual US multi-discipline robotics expo whose combat division runs six standard weight classes (150g through 250lb) plus parallel walking-bonus classes at 100% extra weight and separate 1lb/3lb autonomous divisions. It has one of the most detailed public banned-weapon and judging-scoring rulesets of any hobby organization.

entities.name: BattleBots Design & Safety Rules
entities.summary: BattleBots is the flagship US televised combat robotics league, running one professional heavyweight division at 250 lb ready-to-fight (up to 500 lb for a qualifying articulated-leg walker). Lifting/flipping weapons must pass a functional test lifting 250 lb to 12 inches before being allowed to compete, and every robot goes through a rigorous in-person tech and safety inspection ('the box') before being cleared to fight.

entities.name: Antweight World Series Rules (UK)
entities.summary: The Antweight World Series (AWS) is the primary UK/European antweight ruleset, run in association with Bristol Bot Builders. It defines UK-scale classes far lighter than their US namesakes (Antweight 150g roller / 225g non-roller, Fleaweight 75g/113g, Nanoweight 25g/38g), a detailed banned-weapons list, and specific electrical/radio/battery safety rules distinct from US SPARC practice.

entities.name: Fighting Robots Association (FRA) Build Rules
entities.summary: The Fighting Robots Association publishes build rules used across a number of UK and continental European combat events, complementing the AWS antweight-specific ruleset with guidance that spans a wider range of weight classes and general safety practice for European events.

entities.name: RoboWars Australia Weight Classes & Rules
entities.summary: The Australian combat robotics scene (RoboWars Australia) follows essentially the same SPARC-style weight ladder used in the US and Canada, not the lighter UK/AWS scale: Antweight is 1 lb (454 g), matching US antweight rather than the UK's 150 g class. Australia's ladder additionally runs a Super Heavyweight class at 340 lb (154 kg), one tier above the common 220 lb heavyweight, plus a separate off-arena 'UltiBot' outdoor-terrain division.

entities.name: RoboGames
entities.summary: The largest general-purpose robotics competition and expo in the US, featuring a large combat robotics division alongside other robot sports. Combat weight classes run from 150g fairyweight through 250lb heavyweight, plus walking-bonus and autonomous divisions.

entities.name: BattleBots (TV Series & Live Events)
entities.summary: The best-known televised combat robotics competition, running a single professional 250lb heavyweight division (up to 500lb for qualifying walkers) with a dedicated fighting arena (the BattleBox) and celebrity/expert judging panels.

entities.name: Motorama
entities.summary: One of the longest-running US combat robotics events, historically held in Pennsylvania and now associated with Doswell, Virginia. Runs SPARC-aligned weight classes with a strong antweight/beetleweight/plastic-antweight community presence, and is a well-known season-opener on the US hobby calendar.

entities.name: Antweight World Series Championship (UK)
entities.summary: The championship event of the UK Antweight World Series circuit, the top competitive target for UK-scale 150g antweight, fleaweight, and nanoweight builders, run under the AWS ruleset via Bristol Bot Builders.

entities.name: Walker/Non-Wheeled Weight Bonus
entities.summary: A weight allowance given to robots that move without continuous rolling or cam-driven contact with the floor, since true walking mechanisms are heavier and less efficient than wheels for a given weight. Typical bonus is +100% (double weight) for a full walker and roughly +50% for shufflers/other non-wheeled-but-not-strict-walker locomotion.

entities.name: Multibot / Clusterbot
entities.summary: A single competition entry made of two or more physically separate robots controlled together as one 'weapon system,' sharing the weight limit of their class. Rules typically require all sub-units to be destroyed/immobilized for the team to lose, and extra weight allowance can apply if all sub-units are walkers.

entities.name: Tap-Out
entities.summary: A rule allowing a robot's driver to voluntarily concede a match (usually by a verbal call or a pit-crew signal to the referee) to stop the fight before further damage or danger occurs. Common across NHRL, SPARC-style events, and AWS.

entities.name: Knockout (KO) / Immobility Count
entities.summary: A robot that shows no controlled, purposeful movement for a set count (commonly 10 seconds) is ruled 'out' and the match ends in the opponent's favor, similar to a boxing knockout. AWS/UK rules use a 10-second countdown; many US events use similar counts, sometimes referee-judged rather than a strict clock.

entities.name: Pit / Arena Hazard
entities.summary: A hole, drop, or automated hazard (spikes, hammers, saws) built into some arenas that can end a match instantly if a robot falls in or is forced into it — commonly touching the bottom of a pit is an automatic loss under UK/AWS-style rules. Larger UK 'house robot'-style arenas historically had multiple hazards; most hobby-class US arenas are simpler flat boxes without hazards.

entities.name: Weapon Lock
entities.summary: A required, highly visible physical device (often neon orange) that mechanically prevents a weapon (spinner, lifter, hammer) from moving while the robot is powered but outside the arena — during pit setup, transport, and pre-match staging. Inspectors check that it is fitted before power-on and removed only once the robot is placed in the arena.

entities.name: Radio Fail-Safe
entities.summary: A required behavior of the receiver/ESC system: if the transmitter signal is lost (turned off, out of range, or interfered with), all motion (drive and weapon) must stop automatically rather than continue at the last commanded value. Nearly universal requirement (SPARC, NHRL, RoboGames, AWS) and is actively tested by inspectors turning off the transmitter during check-in.

entities.name: Removable Link / Master Power Switch
entities.summary: A tool-free, externally accessible way to fully disconnect the main battery from the rest of the robot. Many rulesets require both a switch (for routine on/off) and, for larger classes, a physically removable link/jumper as a secondary, more certain isolation method that a marshal or the builder can pull in an emergency without needing the switch to still be functional.

entities.name: Plastic-Class Material Restriction
entities.summary: The defining rule of plastic antweight/plastic beetleweight: the entire structure must be built from an approved list of 3D-printable/injection-moldable plastics, excluding electronics, motors, fasteners, and bearings. This keeps cost and damage low, which is why plastic antweight is recommended as a first build.

entities.name: Pinning Time Limit
entities.summary: A rule capping how long one robot may hold or corner an opponent without active combat, to prevent stalling wins. Typical limits: 15-20 seconds before the referee orders separation or the pin counts against the pinning robot; cornering an opponent against the wall is generally treated the same as a physical pin.

entities.name: Tethered Detachable Weapon Rule
entities.summary: A safety rule requiring that any weapon part designed to detach in combat (e.g. a thrown hammer head or a shattering disc meant to break away) remain physically tethered to the main robot body, with a maximum tether length, to prevent uncontrolled projectiles reaching the crowd or arena walls.

entities.name: Judges' Decision
entities.summary: When a match runs its full time without a knockout or tap-out, a panel of judges (commonly 3) decides the winner using weighted criteria, most often a mix of damage dealt, aggression/control shown, and (in some rulesets) strategy. RoboGames formalizes this as Aggression (max 5 pts) + Damage (max 6 pts) per judge, for 33 total points across a 3-judge panel.

entities.name: LiPo Battery Safety Handling
entities.summary: A set of near-universal pit-safety practices for lithium-polymer batteries used in combat robots: charge only in a fireproof LiPo bag or vented metal/ammo box, never leave a charging battery unattended, inspect for swelling/puncture damage before every use, and store/transport in fire-resistant bags. Several major events (e.g. RoboGames 2017) have had LiPo fires in the pits, which is why fireproof bags are now commonly mandatory rather than optional.
